nodes.label: Jay Winter
nodes.date_label: Sites of Memory, Sites of Mourning (1995) · Remembering War (2006) · War Beyond Words (2017)

nodes.label: Frederick Jackson Turner
nodes.date_label: “The Significance of the Frontier in American History” (1893) · Rise of the New West (1906) · The Frontier in American History (1920)
nodes.description: A historian whose frontier interpretation linked western settlement to American institutions and democracy. His presidential address also called for historians to combine economic, political, geographical and social inquiries. The settler-centred language of available land is his historical premise, with Indigenous dispossession obscured by that formulation.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: “The Significance of the Frontier in American History” (1893); Rise of the New West (1906); The Frontier in American History (1920).

nodes.date_label: One Vast Winter Count (2003) · The Scratch of a Pen (2006) · The Indian World of George Washington (2018)

edges.relationship: Examines how art, museums and silence mediate remembrance of modern war.
edges.evidence_note: Own interview treats memory through changing forms of representation; remembrance is not equated with accurate or therapeutic recovery.

edges.relationship: Contributes to the Historial museum’s international research and display of the Great War.
edges.evidence_note: Own museum answers explain proposing a research centre and a wider war history, with many collaborators; he is not credited as sole creator.

edges.relationship: Shows marriage roles and the balance between spouses changing historically.
edges.evidence_note: Own interview compares marital hierarchy, parity and privacy; not a timeless claim about every household.

edges.relationship: Analyzes marriage as a public legal status as well as a consensual relationship.
edges.evidence_note: Own interview explains state authorization and changing marriage/divorce rules. This is historical interpretation, not legal advice or a reading of the complete book.

edges.relationship: Defends attention to ordinary voices and contingent events without making eighteenth-century life merely a prelude to 1789.
edges.evidence_note: Own opening answers expressly reject teleology and emphasize possibilities not realized.

edges.relationship: Argues for historical movement and moments of imbalance against invariant accounts of masculine/feminine domination.
edges.evidence_note: Own response on Héritier combines admiration with criticism; disagreement is specific, not rejection of feminist history.

edges.relationship: Offers regimes of historicity as a heuristic for varying relations among past, present and future.
edges.evidence_note: Own ENS answer defines an instrument of inquiry rather than universal stages every society must pass through.

edges.relationship: Diagnoses presentism as a shifting dominance of the present in relations to past and future.
edges.evidence_note: Own ENS explanation links diagnosis to observing discordant times after the Berlin Wall; not a claim historical time literally stopped.

edges.relationship: Connects the postwar baby boom to marriage timing, employment constraints and policy as well as prosperity.
edges.evidence_note: Own PBS answer gives multiple mechanisms; does not reduce family history to fertility statistics.

edges.relationship: Shows domestic gender ideals entwined with Cold War security and constrained employment options.
edges.evidence_note: Own PBS answers distinguish the heterosexual suburban ideal from married women’s continuing paid work.

edges.relationship: Places Detroit’s urban crisis in changes already under way during the 1940s and 1950s.
edges.evidence_note: Own 1999 answers reject making 1960s social programmes the originating cause and identify industrial restructuring and housing practices.

edges.relationship: Connects racial inequality to discrimination in jobs and housing alongside the reorganization of industrial work.
edges.evidence_note: Own transcript distinguishes racialized consequences of capital flight from an explanation based on economic change alone.

edges.relationship: Explains American political development through western settlement and changing social forces.
edges.evidence_note: Primary frontier opening and 1910 address ground the interpretation; “free land” is a settler premise that obscures Indigenous sovereignty.

edges.relationship: Calls for combined economic, political, geographic and social inquiry rather than isolated specialist explanations.
edges.evidence_note: Read 1910 address explicitly argues that human social factors are varied and complex; no claim Turner founded later comparative historical sociology.

edges.relationship: Shows immigration law reorganizing racial boundaries through quotas and categorical Asian exclusion.
edges.evidence_note: Author’s quoted account and interview answers distinguish European national classifications from exclusions directed at Asians.

edges.relationship: Treats unauthorized immigration as a historically produced consequence of restriction and enforcement.
edges.evidence_note: Interview examines1924 and1965 changes; it does not treat every migration history as the same or offer current legal guidance.

edges.relationship: Examines the historical making of deserving/undeserving poverty classifications.
edges.evidence_note: Own quoted statements explain the continuing moralization of poverty; does not endorse those categories as natural differences.

edges.relationship: Connects poorhouse history to later shelters and the institutional management of poverty.
edges.evidence_note: Own short interview questions punitive solutions while acknowledging material changes over time, rather than equating all institutions.

edges.relationship: Centres Native peoples and sovereignty within the history of the early United States.
edges.evidence_note: Own interview explicitly argues Native history is integral to American history; this is not a claim of Indigenous identity or authority.

edges.relationship: Uses Washington’s dealings with Native peoples to reconstruct a contingent era of nation-building and dispossession.
edges.evidence_note: Own interview distinguishes the project from biography in the usual sense and contrasts promises of sovereignty with policies eroding it.
